lead: A random process attaches a random variable to every time instant. One run of the experiment gives one whole sample path, not just one number. Queue length through a day, voltage from a sensor, and the count of arrivals at a UPI server are examples. Engineers use it to describe uncertainty that changes with time. This chapter defines the index set and state space, shows how to read a sample path, and classifies processes by time, state and dependence.
prereq: You need: random variables and distributions (see Unit 2, Probability and Random Variables), especially pmf, pdf and expectation.

blocks.text: A random process is a family of random variables {X(t): t ∈ T}. The set T is the index set, the allowed time values. The set S is the state space, the allowed values of X(t). If T is countable we call it discrete time; if T is an interval we call continuous time. Some syllabi say stochastic process for random process.

Fix one outcome ω of the underlying experiment. The function t ↦ X(t, ω) is one sample path or realization. Some syllabi say sample function. At one fixed time t, X(t) is a random variable across outcomes; the collection of these values across outcomes is the ensemble. One experiment gives one whole path, not the full ensemble.

items: T answers when: the time values where the process is observed.
S answers what value: the possible states of X(t).
A sample path is one observed graph of X(t) against t.
The ensemble is the collection of all possible paths at a fixed time.

sections.h3: Time and state classify the process

blocks.text: Two independent choices give four common types. Time asks whether T is countable or an interval. State asks whether S is countable or continuous. The table gives one engineering example for each cell.

blocks.text: The labels describe T and S, not the randomness. A discrete-state process can jump at random times. A continuous-state process can be sampled at fixed times. Put the process in a cell before choosing formulas: countable T uses sequences and sums; interval T uses functions of t; countable S uses a pmf; continuous S uses a pdf.

A second classification asks how X(t) depends on other times. An independent process has X(t) independent of X(s) for all t ≠ s. A Markov process allows dependence, but the future depends on the present state, not on the full past. A stationary process has joint distributions unchanged when all times are shifted by the same amount. Stationarity details are in 7.2; Markov chains start in 7.4.

The Poisson process is the standard continuous-time discrete-state example with independent increments. It is developed in 7.3. A random walk or coin-count process is a discrete-time Markov chain. These names classify dependence, while time and state classify the index set and values.

Ensemble average means averaging across many paths at a fixed t. Time average means averaging one long path along t. They are different objects; ergodicity is the special case where one long record can estimate the ensemble average. That idea is treated in 7.2.

examples.question: A fair coin is tossed repeatedly. Let X(n) be the number of heads after n tosses, with X(0)=0. The toss sequence is H, T, H. (a) Give the index set T and state space S. (b) Write the sample path for n=0,1,2,3. (c) Classify the process by time and state. (d) State X(3).
steps: The index set is the set of time values: T = {0,1,2,...}, because n counts tosses.
The state space is the set of possible head counts: S = {0,1,2,...}.
Start at n=0: X(0)=0, so the path begins with 0.
The sample path is X(0), X(1), X(2), X(3) = 0, 1, 1, 2.
T is countable, so the process is discrete-time. S is countable, so the process is discrete-state. The value after three tosses is X(3)=2 heads.
examples.answer: The index set is T={0,1,2,...}, the state space is S={0,1,2,...}, the sample path is 0,1,1,2, and X(3)=2 heads after three tosses; the process is discrete-time and discrete-state.

traps: The state space S is the set of values X(t), not the set of time values T. In the coin example, n comes from T but the path values 0,1,1,2 come from S.
Discrete time does not mean discrete state. A voltage sampled every second has discrete time and continuous state.
Continuous time does not mean continuous state. A Poisson count has continuous time and discrete state {0,1,2,...}.
Markov is not the same as independent or stationary. A Markov process may have dependence through the present state; stationarity is a separate shift-invariance property.
An ensemble average and a time average are different. One long sample path does not automatically give the ensemble average; ergodicity is the special case where it does.

quiz.q: Define the index set T and the state space S of a random process X(t).
quiz.a: T is the set of allowed time values where X(t) is observed. S is the set of allowed values that X(t) can take.

quiz.q: Why is a random process not just one random variable?
quiz.a: A random variable gives one uncertain number. A random process gives a random variable at every time t in T. One experiment therefore produces a whole sample path, not one number.

quiz.q: A coin is tossed four times in the order H, T, T, H. Let X(n) be the number of heads after n tosses with X(0)=0. Write the sample path for n=0,1,2,3,4 and give X(4).
quiz.a: Start X(0)=0. H gives X(1)=1. T gives X(2)=1. T gives X(3)=1. H gives X(4)=2. The path is 0,1,1,1,2 and X(4)=2 heads.

quiz.q: A call centre counts the number of incoming calls once every minute. Classify the process by time and state.
quiz.a: Calls are counted at discrete minute marks, so T is discrete. The count takes values 0,1,2,..., so S is discrete. It is discrete-time, discrete-state.

quiz.q: A process has continuous time T and state space S={0,1}. Can it be a Markov process? Explain in two lines.
quiz.a: Yes. A process can have continuous time and a discrete two-value state. The Markov property concerns dependence on the past, not whether T or S is continuous. A two-state continuous-time Markov chain is an example.

quiz.q: In the repeated fair-coin process where X(n) is the number of heads after n tosses, is X(n) Markov? Give the reason using the next value.
quiz.a: Yes. Given X(n)=k, the next value is k+1 with probability 1/2 if the next toss is H, and k with probability 1/2 if T. This rule uses only k and the next toss, not the earlier toss history.

quiz.q: Distinguish a sample path from an ensemble average.
quiz.a: A sample path is one observed function of time for one outcome. An ensemble average is an average across many outcomes at one fixed time t. One path does not by itself give the ensemble average.

beyond: Not for the exam. Random processes model queue lengths in cloud servers, noise in radio receivers, and price ticks in finance. Search terms: stochastic process, Markov chain, Poisson process, ergodicity, Monte Carlo simulation. Simulation is often the first tool when formulas are hard.
